name: Somnath Temple, Prabhas Patan
deity: Shiva as Somanatha, Lord of the Moon — the first of the twelve Jyotirlingas
period: An ancient tirtha of Prabhasa on the Saurashtra coast; rebuilt many times, the present temple consecrated in 1951
dynasty: Chaulukya (Solanki) and later; present temple by the Shree Somnath Trust
summary: On the shore of the Arabian Sea at Prabhas Patan, Somnath honours Shiva as Lord of the Moon — first of the twelve Jyotirlingas, a shrine rebuilt again and again across a thousand years.

sections.history: Prabhasa, where three rivers meet the sea on the Saurashtra coast, has been a place of pilgrimage since epic times, and the Dvadasha Jyotirlinga Stotram opens its roll of the twelve Jyotirlingas with "Somanatha in Saurashtra." The temple's story is one of repeated loss and renewal. It was sacked by Mahmud of Ghazni in 1025–26, rebuilt by the Chaulukya (Solanki) kings of Gujarat — among them Kumarapala in the 12th century — and damaged and raised again more than once in the centuries that followed. In 1783 Ahilyabai Holkar built a separate Shiva temple close by, where worship continued. After Independence a public trust undertook a complete rebuilding on the ancient site, and the Jyotirlinga was consecrated by President Rajendra Prasad on 11 May 1951.
sections.architecture: The present temple, designed by the master builder Prabhashankar Sompura, revives the Maru-Gurjara manner of the old Solanki temples of Gujarat. Its plan, called Kailash Mahameru Prasad, runs from the sanctum through an assembly hall to a dance pavilion, every surface worked in carved sandstone. The shikhara rises about fifty metres and is crowned by a kalasha said to weigh ten tonnes. On the sea wall stands the Baan Stambh, an arrow pillar whose inscription holds that no land lies between this shore and the South Pole along its line.
sections.legends: The name means Lord of Soma, the Moon. The Puranas tell that Chandra married the twenty-seven daughters of Daksha but loved only Rohini, and the slighted father cursed him to waste away. Fading, the Moon came to Prabhasa and worshipped Shiva, who softened the curse so that Chandra would wane and wax in turn — the rhythm of every lunar month. Here, it is said, Shiva remained as Somanatha. Prabhasa is also linked with the last days of Krishna, whose departure from the world tradition places at nearby Bhalka Tirtha.
sections.festivals: Maha Shivaratri brings the largest crowds, with worship through the night. The month of Shravan is especially sacred, its Mondays drawing pilgrims from across Gujarat and beyond. A large fair gathers on the shore at Kartik Purnima, and the Triveni Sangam fills with bathers on auspicious days. Confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Somnath is best seen as the sun goes down, when the evening aarti sounds within and the sandstone spire glows against the sea. Walk out to the Baan Stambh to hear the waves on the wall, then visit the Ahilyabai temple, the Triveni Sangam and Bhalka Tirtha nearby. An evening light-and-sound presentation retells the temple's long history.

visit.timings: Open daily from early morning to night, with aartis at dawn, midday and evening; confirm timings locally, as hours extend at Maha Shivaratri and in Shravan.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional dress is expected, with shoulders and knees covered; footwear is removed before entering.
visit.photography: Mobile phones, cameras and bags are deposited at the entrance under security rules, and photography is not permitted inside the temple; follow posted rules and staff guidance.
visit.gettingThere: Somnath is about 6 km from Veraval in Gir Somnath district, Gujarat, and is served by Somnath and Veraval railway stations. The nearest airports are Diu (about 85 km) and Rajkot (about 190 km); Ahmedabad is about 400 km away by road.
